Newborn Care

Sticky eyes in newborns: discharge, blocked tear ducts and treatment

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Yellow crust on a newborn’s eyelashes can come from tears that do not drain well, but discharge can also accompany an infection. Colour alone cannot tell you the cause. A newborn with red, swollen or tender eyes needs prompt medical assessment; cleaning should not become a reason to postpone it.

Start with the baby, not the colour

Notice when the discharge began, whether one or both eyes are affected, and whether there is persistent watering, redness, swelling or discomfort. Tell the clinician about feeding, alertness, temperature and any birth or infection history. A photograph or the shade of the discharge cannot reliably distinguish a blocked duct from conjunctivitis.

Seek an urgent assessment now for red, sticky eyes in a baby under 30 days old, rather than waiting several days for cleaning to work. Newborn eye infection can threaten sight or involve other parts of the body. If a clinician has already diagnosed uncomplicated tear-duct obstruction, follow that care plan but seek new advice for changed symptoms.

How a blocked tear duct causes stickiness

Tears are made in a gland above the outer side of the eye. After coating the surface, they enter tiny openings near the inner eyelid corners and pass through channels and a tear sac into a duct that drains to the nose. A small membrane may not yet have opened, or another part of this drainage system may be narrow or incompletely developed.

When drainage is restricted, tears can spill onto the cheek and mucus can collect on lashes, sometimes sticking the lids together after sleep. One or both eyes can be affected. Stickiness does not by itself prove an infection, but blocked drainage and infection can coexist. Unusual light sensitivity, a cloudy cornea or an enlarged-looking eye needs prompt specialist assessment for other causes, including childhood glaucoma.

What improvement over time can mean

Blocked tear drainage is common, but estimates vary according to whether studies count symptoms or an unopened passage. AAPOS reports symptoms in more than 5% of infants and improvement in about 90% during the first year. These are group estimates, not a promise that every baby will recover by four to six months or need surgery at a particular birthday.

Symptoms may come and go and worsen with a cold, nasal congestion, wind or cold weather. Avoid direct irritants and discuss persistent problems at follow-up. Assessment should not be delayed until a year of age: the diagnosis needs checking earlier, while decisions about continued observation or a procedure depend on symptoms, repeated infections and the eye specialist’s findings.

Clean the outside of the eye gently

Wash and dry your hands before and after care. For crusts, use clean cotton wool or a soft clean pad moistened with water that has been boiled and allowed to cool. Gently wipe the lashes and skin from the nose outward, using a fresh pad for each eye and a clean pad for further passes. Do not rub the eyeball, force stuck lids apart or use hot water.

Keep towels and face cloths separate when infection is possible. Do not put tea, homemade mixtures or someone else’s leftover drops into the eye. Do not use breast milk as a substitute for assessment or prescribed treatment. External cleaning can remove crust and improve comfort; it neither establishes the diagnosis nor cures a serious infection.

Massage should be shown for your baby

For confirmed uncomplicated obstruction, a clinician may teach tear-sac massage near the inner corner of the eye, with a downward movement alongside the nose. Ask them to show the position, pressure and frequency and to watch you repeat it. Do not press on the eyeball or copy a forceful technique from a photograph; instructions should suit the child’s diagnosis.

Massage may help drainage but is not guaranteed to open every blockage. Do not massage a painful, red or swollen inner eye corner. Stop and seek urgent advice for new swelling; a tender red lump there may be a serious tear-sac infection and needs emergency assessment. Cleaning or massage must never delay care for a newborn’s red, inflamed eye or an unwell baby.

Conjunctivitis is a different problem

Conjunctivitis inflames the surface over the white of the eye and inside the eyelids. Redness, puffy or tender lids and pus can occur. Causes include bacteria, viruses and irritation; appearances and the day symptoms start overlap. Do not restrict concern to the first 14 days or assume that a white-looking eye rules out every problem.

Some infections are acquired around birth, including chlamydia, gonorrhoea and herpes; other bacteria are not sexually transmitted. The person who gave birth may have had no symptoms. Share relevant pregnancy screening, treatment and birth information without blame. The team may take eye samples and assess the baby more widely, including for infection beyond the eye when indicated.

Treatment depends on the cause

A prescriber may select antibiotic drops or ointment for certain bacterial infections or troublesome discharge with a blocked duct. These medicines do not mechanically open the duct and should not be used indefinitely or borrowed from another person. Antibiotics do not treat viral infections; suspected herpes needs a different specialist treatment plan.

Chlamydial and gonococcal newborn eye infections need systemic treatment, not eye drops alone. Depending on the diagnosis, medicine may be given by mouth, injection or vein, with hospital care or follow-up. Some treatments need monitoring in very young infants. Follow the prescribed course and review plan; the parents and relevant partners may also need testing and treatment when a particular infection is identified.

When probing or a stent is considered

If symptoms remain troublesome around or after the first year, or are severe or repeatedly infected earlier, an ophthalmologist may discuss probing. A thin instrument is passed through the drainage passage to open it, sometimes with irrigation, balloon widening or a small temporary tube or stent. This is a specialist procedure, never something to try at home.

Timing and anaesthesia depend on age, the procedure and the child. Some young infants can have office probing with numbing drops; older children often need general anaesthesia for safety. Many procedures work well, but repeat treatment can be needed. Rarely, more complex surgery such as dacryocystorhinostomy creates another drainage route. Ask about alternatives, risks, stent care and the follow-up plan; persistence alone does not make every child’s operation identical.

Recognize a tear-sac complication

A painful, red, swollen lump by the inner eye corner, especially with increased discharge, can be dacryocystitis: an infection of the tear sac. Seek emergency assessment immediately; do not wait for fever or for all symptoms to appear. Oral or intravenous antibiotics and sometimes hospital care are needed. Do not squeeze or massage the swelling.

A bluish swelling near that corner may instead be a trapped-fluid swelling called a dacryocystocele, which also needs prompt specialist assessment. It can be associated with a cyst inside the nose and interfere with breathing. Breathing difficulty is an emergency. Neither the colour of a lump nor an online image can establish which condition is present.

When to use emergency care and how to follow up

Seek immediate emergency care for breathing difficulty, blue, grey or unusually pale colour, a floppy or unresponsive baby, difficulty waking, a seizure, a temperature of 38°C or higher under 3 months, a temperature below 36°C, or no urine for 12 hours. A red eye with apparent new vision change, pain on looking at light, an injury or chemical exposure also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

For poor feeding, new eye redness, discharge or swelling, or any concern about your newborn, contact a clinician promptly even without those emergency signs. Keep the planned review for confirmed obstruction. Bring questions about the diagnosis, safe care, what change should trigger an earlier visit and when persistent symptoms warrant an eye specialist. You do not need to wait for a fixed month or colour change to ask for help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Arrange prompt assessment of a newborn’s discharge and urgent review for red, sticky eyes. Tell the team the baby’s age, feeding, alertness, temperature and relevant birth or infection history.

For confirmed uncomplicated obstruction, ask for a demonstration of external cleaning and any massage. Use only this baby’s prescribed medicine and stop manipulation of a painful or swollen inner corner.

Keep follow-up and ask when persistent symptoms merit ophthalmology review or a procedure. Seek emergency help for the warning signs instead of waiting for cleaning, massage or an app record to show improvement.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record when discharge began, symptoms, appointments and questions for the care team. It cannot diagnose infection, identify an obstructed duct, assess sight, teach safe probing or decide that urgent care can wait.

When to seek help

A newborn’s red, sticky eye needs urgent assessment. A painful red swelling at the inner eye corner needs emergency assessment; do not massage it. Breathing difficulty, blue/grey or unusually pale colour, floppiness, poor response, difficulty waking, seizure, 38°C or higher under 3 months, below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours need immediate emergency care. A red eye with vision change, light sensitivity, injury or chemical exposure also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance. No home probing, borrowed drops or delayed care while trying remedies.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Yellow discharge is a symptom, not a diagnosis; newborn red, sticky eyes need urgent assessment.
  • Most uncomplicated blocked tear ducts improve, but the course and need for a procedure vary.
  • Clean lashes gently and use only clinician-demonstrated massage for the confirmed condition.
  • Eye drops do not open a duct; some neonatal infections need systemic specialist treatment.
  • A painful red inner-corner lump or an unwell baby can need emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

Is yellow discharge normal in a newborn?

It is common with blocked tear drainage, but should not automatically be dismissed as harmless. Redness, tender or swollen lids, persistent discharge or an unwell baby need assessment. Red, sticky eyes under 30 days need urgent medical review.

What causes the discharge?

A passage draining tears to the nose may not have opened fully, allowing tears and mucus to collect. Infection or irritation can also cause discharge, and more than one problem may coexist. A clinician should check the cause rather than choosing treatment by colour.

Will a blocked tear duct clear by itself?

Often it improves during the first year, and some take longer. Four to six months is not a guaranteed deadline. Follow the care and review plan; ongoing troublesome symptoms, infections or uncertainty about the diagnosis justify earlier advice.

How should I massage the tear duct?

Ask a clinician to confirm the diagnosis and demonstrate the position, downward movement, pressure and frequency for your baby. Do not press the eyeball or massage a painful, red or swollen inner corner. A tender red lump there needs emergency assessment.

Can I clean the eye without drops?

Gentle external cleaning with cooled boiled water and a fresh clean pad for each eye can remove crust. It does not replace assessment for a newborn’s inflamed eye. Do not use tea, homemade preparations, borrowed drops or breast milk in place of necessary medical care.

Does every infection only need antibiotic eye drops?

No. Treatment depends on the cause. Chlamydial and gonococcal neonatal infections require systemic treatment; viruses and herpes need different decisions. The baby may need samples, a wider assessment and follow-up. Do not select a medicine yourself.

Must every persistent blocked duct have surgery at one year?

No. Symptoms, infections, age and anatomy guide whether to observe longer, probe or use another procedure. The specialist should explain anaesthesia, likely benefit, repeat-treatment possibility and any stent care. Never attempt to open the duct at home.

Which signs need emergency help?

A painful red inner-corner swelling needs emergency assessment even without fever. So do breathing difficulty, blue/grey or unusually pale colour, floppiness, reduced response, difficulty waking, seizure, 38°C or higher under 3 months, below 36°C or no urine for 12 hours. A red eye with vision change, light sensitivity, injury or chemical exposure also needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself; ask another driver or call an ambulance.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
